posts.name: InvestmentGuru
posts.text: The government is out telling everyone to stock up for three days, like it is a brand new idea, and the stores are about to do very well out of it. I went down to my basement today and found ten packs of water and shelves of tins and bins, and I did not buy a single one of them. My wife did. We never had that much water or food in this house before, and now she has us ready before the government even finished the announcement. That is the thing about fear, it sells, and it sells fast, water first and everything else after. The advice itself is not even new, it has been the same 72-hour guidance for years, but say it on the news in November and suddenly everyone is a prepper. In my house, my wife was the prepper. The question is whether the shelves are still full when everyone else gets there.

This slide from the Anthropic IPO roadshow was a big factor in my decision to leave. It’s an insane plot and I’m surprised they made it public.

It shows the compute efficiency of pretraining over time. The y-axis is a **log scale**: they are seeing continued superexponential algorithmic progress.

Mythos was not a one-time deviation, but a point on a superexponential. They could already retrain Mythos with a fraction of the compute originally needed.

It doesn’t strictly imply a software-only intelligence explosion- they have been spending more on R+D. But algorithmic improvements do not require ridiculous creative genius and are on the verge of being automated. You do the math.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
The last 20 years have been a fascinating test of capitalism and the narratives around it.

The GFC backlash was deserved. Banks made reckless and often predatory loans, then got bailed out. That was corporatism at its worst, and I was critical of it at the time. Some of you might remember I was basically in favor of Keynesianism on steroids back then, because the economy had a massive demand hole to fill.

Covid was different. Lockdowns caused supply shocks, and then we met those shocks with trillions in fiscal stimulus. Too much spending chasing too little supply. High inflation was the predictable result. That was big government at work trying to fix a problem and making it worse in many ways. Yet many people still blame “capitalism” for the outcome.

Two very different crises. Same scapegoat. It’s a good reminder that we all fit the facts to the story we already believe.
